blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer array `nums` of non-negative values and an integer `k`, split `nums` into `k` non-empty **contiguous** pieces so that the **largest piece sum is as small as possible**. Return that smallest possible largest sum.

blocks.alt: nums 7, 2, 5, 10, 8 split into k = 2 pieces. Splitting after 5 gives 7 + 2 + 5 = 14 and 10 + 8 = 18: the largest is 18, the best possible. With a limit of 17, greedy pieces are 7, 2, 5 (14), then 10 (adding 8 would pass 17), then 8: three pieces, too many. So 18 is the first limit that needs at most 2 pieces.

blocks.text: The idea: "minimize the largest" means search the limit

Fix a **limit** and ask: can the array be cut into at most `k` pieces, none summing past the limit? Greedy answers it — extend the current piece while it stays within the limit, otherwise start a new one. Fewer than k pieces is fine too, because any piece can be split further without raising the largest sum. A higher limit never needs more pieces, so the answers flip from no to yes once. The limit is at least the **biggest value** (it has to fit in some piece) and at most the **total**. This is exactly Capacity To Ship Packages, with pieces for days.

`best[j][i]` is the smallest largest-sum when the first `i` values are cut into `j` pieces. The last piece is `nums[p..i−1]` for some `p`, so take the best over all `p` of the larger of `best[j−1][p]` and that piece's sum (from prefix sums).
**Time O(k · n²), space O(k · n).** Correct and a classic DP, but slow for n = 1000 and k = 50.

blocks.caption: At each limit, cut the array greedily and count the pieces; at most k means the limit works.

blocks.text: **Time O(n log(total)), space O(1).** The search finds the smallest limit that works, and that limit is always an actual piece sum: if no piece hit it exactly, a smaller limit would work too.

blocks.alt: Dynamic programming: O(k · n²) time, O(k · n) space. Binary search on the limit: O(n log total) time, O(1) space.

items: **k = n** — every value alone: the biggest value.
**Large sums** — the total can pass 2³¹; Java and C++ use 64-bit sums.
**Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days** — the same problem in different words.
**Painter's Partition** and **Book Allocation** — classic names for the same search.
**Divide Chocolate** — maximize the smallest piece instead: a last-yes search.
